claims.text: Substitutional alloying with elements of varying atomic radii can introduce controlled lattice distortion in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The introduced lattice distortion can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
A balanced composition in a eutectic high-entropy alloy can achieve optimal mechanical properties.
A moderate level of lattice distortion can be introduced without compromising alloy stability.
Appropriate selection of substitutional elements can avoid unwanted precipitate formation.
Optimizing processing temperature and cooling rate can retain the desired eutectic microstructure.
Lattice distortion can cause the formation of defects such as dislocations.
Introduced dislocations can interact with one another and with the alloy microstructure.
Lattice distortion provides additional obstacles to dislocation movement and thereby increases strength.
Controlled introduction of defects enhances ductility by enabling more efficient plastic deformation.
The intervention will increase yield strength by at least 10% relative to the baseline alloy.
The intervention will improve ductility by at least 15% relative to the baseline alloy.
The comparator should be a compositionally balanced, processing-optimized eutectic high-entropy alloy without intentional lattice distortion.
The proposed effect should hold for eutectic high-entropy alloys with moderate to high entropy of mixing.
The proposed effect should hold at temperatures and strain rates relevant to structural applications.
Failure to obtain a significant improvement in both strength and ductility relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
